# Questions for Today

- What comparison would allow us to measure employment discrimination?
- What does an audit experiment hold constant? What does it change?
- What does the research design allow us to say?
- How certain are we about the result?
- Does a result from Milwaukee in 2001 travel to other places, people, jobs,
  employers, and times?
- What do we learn when the same basic design is used for more than 83,000
  applications?

The code is provided. Before running each chunk, decide what comparison it is
making and what you expect to see. After running it, return to the question.
The point is not to remember the syntax. The point is to use the analysis to
decide what the data allow us to say.

# Does a Criminal Record Reduce the Chance of a Callback?

In this exercise, we analyze the causal effects of a criminal record on the job
prospects of white and Black job applicants. The exercise begins with Devah
Pager's “The Mark of a Criminal Record.”

Pager wanted to know how a criminal record affects employment opportunities.
She also wanted to know whether the effect was the same for Black and white
applicants.

Why is that question difficult to answer using ordinary employment records?

What might differ between people with and without criminal records besides the
record itself?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

# Pager's Audit Experiment

Pager hired two pairs of men to apply for entry-level jobs in Milwaukee. One
pair was Black and one pair was white. The testers were matched within each
pair on physical appearance and self-presentation.

Within each pair, Pager randomly varied which tester reported a felony drug
conviction. The pair alternated which applicant presented the criminal record
each week.

What is the treatment?

What is the outcome?

What was randomized? What was not randomized?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

What comparison identifies the effect of a criminal record among white
applicants? What comparison identifies it among Black applicants?

Can we identify the effect of race in exactly the same way? Why or why not?

## What Does a Callback Measure?

The outcome is whether an employer called the tester back after the
application.

Does a callback measure whether someone was hired? Does it measure how the
employer would treat the person after hiring? Does it tell us why the employer
made the decision?

What part of employment discrimination can this outcome reveal?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

## Load and Inspect the Pager Data

The file `criminalrecord.csv` contains 695 of the 699 applications in the
study. Four cases were redacted, so our results differ slightly from the
published results.

```{r load-pager-data}
library(tidyverse)

audit = read.csv("criminalrecord.csv")

glimpse(audit)
```

What is one row? Which variables identify the treatment, outcome, and race of
the tester?

## What Pattern Do You Expect?

Write down the expected ordering before calculating anything.

- Which group should have the highest callback rate?
- Which group should have the lowest?
- If criminal records matter, what should we observe within each race?
- If race matters, what should we observe within each criminal-record group?

## Calculate the Four Callback Rates

The labels are created so we do not have to remember what 0 and 1 mean while
interpreting the result.

```{r calculate-pager-rates}
pager_rates = audit |>
  mutate(
    Race = if_else(black == 1, "Black", "White"),
    CriminalRecord = if_else(crimrec == 1, "Record", "No record")
  ) |>
  group_by(Race, CriminalRecord) |>
  summarize(
    Applications = n(),
    CallbackRate = mean(callback),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

pager_rates
```

What do you observe?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

## Plot the Comparison We Care About

The plot uses the same four rates. Criminal record is on the horizontal axis
because that is the randomized treatment. Race distinguishes the two pairs of
testers.

```{r plot-pager-rates}
ggplot(
  pager_rates,
  aes(x = CriminalRecord, y = CallbackRate, fill = Race)
) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, .4),
    breaks = seq(0, .4, by = .1),
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "How Do Callback Rates Vary by Race and Criminal Record?",
    subtitle = "Pager audit experiment, Milwaukee, 2001",
    x = "Criminal record reported to employer",
    y = "Callback rate",
    fill = "Race of tester"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

What comparison is easiest to see in the plot? What remains difficult to
compare?

## Percentage Points or Percent Change?

First calculate the change in percentage points within each race.

```{r pager-percentage-point-effects}
pager_effects = pager_rates |>
  group_by(Race) |>
  summarize(
    NoRecord = CallbackRate[CriminalRecord == "No record"],
    Record = CallbackRate[CriminalRecord == "Record"],
    PercentagePointChange = Record - NoRecord,
    PercentChange = (Record - NoRecord) / NoRecord,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

pager_effects
```

Which race has the larger percentage-point change? Which has the larger
relative change? Why can both answers be correct?

Which summary better answers the question you care about?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

Compare white applicants with a criminal record to Black applicants without a
criminal record.

```{r pager-cross-race-comparison}
pager_rates |>
  filter(
    (Race == "White" & CriminalRecord == "Record") |
      (Race == "Black" & CriminalRecord == "No record")
  )
```

What do we observe?

Is this comparison the randomized effect of race? Return to how the study was
conducted before answering.

### How Certain Are We About That Ordering?

The observed callback rate is higher for white applicants with a criminal
record than for Black applicants without one. Would that ordering appear in
different samples produced by the same process?

We will bootstrap the two groups separately. This is the same resampling
procedure used earlier in the course.

Before running the loop, identify the four steps:

1. Resample white applicants with a record.
2. Resample Black applicants without a record.
3. Calculate the difference in callback rates.
4. Save the difference.

```{r pager-bootstrap}
set.seed(42)

white_record = audit |>
  filter(black == 0, crimrec == 1)

black_no_record = audit |>
  filter(black == 1, crimrec == 0)

pager_bootstrap = NULL

for (i in 1:1000) {
  sampled_white_record = white_record |>
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE)

  sampled_black_no_record = black_no_record |>
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE)

  one_difference = sampled_white_record |>
    summarize(
      Difference = mean(callback) - mean(sampled_black_no_record$callback)
    )

  pager_bootstrap = bind_rows(pager_bootstrap, one_difference)
}
```

Inspect the bootstrap distribution and calculate a 95 percent interval.

```{r inspect-pager-bootstrap}
summary(pager_bootstrap$Difference)

quantile(
  pager_bootstrap$Difference,
  probs = c(.025, .975)
)

pager_bootstrap |>
  summarize(
    ProbabilityWhiteRecordGreater = mean(Difference > 0)
  )
```

```{r plot-pager-bootstrap}
ggplot(pager_bootstrap, aes(x = Difference)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "How Often Is the Difference Greater Than Zero?",
    subtitle = paste(nrow(pager_bootstrap), "bootstrap samples"),
    x = "White with record minus Black without record",
    y = "Number of bootstrap samples"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Is the probability greater than 95 percent? Does the 95 percent interval
exclude zero?

What does this tell us about sampling uncertainty?

Does the bootstrap fix the fact that race was not randomly assigned across
otherwise identical testers?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

# How Far Does Pager's Finding Travel?

Pager made necessary choices when designing the study:

- Milwaukee.
- June through December 2001.
- Entry-level jobs.
- Four 23-year-old male college students.
- In-person applications.
- A felony drug conviction.
- A callback as the outcome.

Choose one decision. How might the result change if Pager made a different
choice?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

Would we expect the same result in Nashville? Twenty years later? For women?
For older applicants? For professional jobs? For a conviction for assault or
tax evasion?

Which concerns are about **scope**? Which are about **temporality**?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

What would a new study need to do to provide a broader foundation for a claim
about employment discrimination?

# What Would a Broader Study Look Like?

The concerns above lead directly to the next study. Patrick Kline, Evan Rose,
and Christopher Walters sent more than 83,000 fictitious applications to more
than 11,000 entry-level jobs at 108 large U.S. employers. Applicant
characteristics were randomly assigned to resumes.

Does that address the limits we identified in Pager's study? Which ones?

What limits remain?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

This is not an exact replication of Pager. It changes how race is communicated,
uses fictitious resumes rather than in-person testers, does not include a
criminal-record treatment, and examines employer contact across many firms and
jobs. It is an extension using the same audit-study logic.

## What Does the Larger Study Cover?

The teaching file keeps all 83,643 applications and the variables needed for
our questions. The employer and job identifiers are anonymized.

```{r load-larger-audit}
large_audit = read.csv(

)

glimpse(large_audit)
```

## Does the Extension Find the Same Basic Pattern?

Return to the design. What is the treatment? What is the outcome?

Before calculating the result, what would make Pager's finding appear more
limited? What result would give the broader claim a more solid foundation?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

```{r calculate-larger-audit-rates}
large_rates = large_audit |>
  group_by(NameRace) |>
  summarize(
    Applications = n(),
    ContactRate = mean(Contact),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

large_rates
```

```{r calculate-larger-audit-gap}
large_rates |>
  summarize(
    Difference = ContactRate[NameRace == "White"] -
      ContactRate[NameRace == "Black"]
  )
```

```{r plot-larger-audit-rates}
ggplot(
  large_rates,
  aes(x = NameRace, y = ContactRate, fill = NameRace)
) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, .3),
    breaks = seq(0, .3, by = .05),
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "How Do Contact Rates Vary by the Race Signaled by a Name?",
    subtitle = "83,643 applications to 108 large U.S. employers",
    x = "Race signaled by applicant name",
    y = "Employer contact rate"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

What do we observe? How many fewer employer contacts would a difference of
about .021 produce for 1,000 applications?

### First Bootstrap: Resample Individual Applications

Use the same bootstrap logic as before. Resample the Black-name and white-name
applications separately, calculate their contact rates, and save the
difference.

```{r application-bootstrap}
set.seed(42)

black_name_applications = large_audit |>
  filter(NameRace == "Black")

white_name_applications = large_audit |>
  filter(NameRace == "White")

application_bootstrap = NULL

for (i in 1:1000) {
  sampled_black = black_name_applications |>
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE)

  sampled_white = white_name_applications |>
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE)

  one_difference = sampled_white |>
    summarize(
      Difference = mean(Contact) - mean(sampled_black$Contact)
    )

  application_bootstrap = bind_rows(
    application_bootstrap,
    one_difference
  )
}
```

```{r inspect-application-bootstrap}
quantile(
  application_bootstrap$Difference,
  probs = c(.025, .975)
)

ggplot(application_bootstrap, aes(x = Difference)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, .04),
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = .1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "What If We Resample Individual Applications?",
    subtitle = paste(nrow(application_bootstrap), "bootstrap samples"),
    x = "White-name minus Black-name contact rate",
    y = "Number of bootstrap samples"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

The interval is narrow. Before believing it, what did this bootstrap assume
about the relationship among the applications?

Were 83,643 applications generated as 83,643 unrelated events? Which
applications went to the same job? Which went to the same employer?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

### Second Bootstrap: Respect the Job-Level Comparison

Applications were sent in groups to the same postings. First calculate a
white–Black contact difference within each job. Then resample jobs.

```{r calculate-job-gaps}
job_gaps = large_audit |>
  group_by(Job) |>
  summarize(
    BlackContact = mean(Contact[NameRace == "Black"]),
    WhiteContact = mean(Contact[NameRace == "White"]),
    Difference = WhiteContact - BlackContact,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(Difference))
```

Why do some jobs lack a within-job difference? Why is a job more sensible to
resample than an individual application?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

```{r job-bootstrap}
set.seed(42)

job_bootstrap = NULL

for (i in 1:1000) {
  one_difference = job_gaps |>
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE) |>
    summarize(Difference = mean(Difference))

  job_bootstrap = bind_rows(job_bootstrap, one_difference)
}

quantile(job_bootstrap$Difference, probs = c(.025, .975))
```

```{r plot-job-bootstrap}
ggplot(job_bootstrap, aes(x = Difference)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, .04),
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = .1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "What Changes When We Resample Jobs?",
    subtitle = paste(nrow(job_bootstrap), "bootstrap samples"),
    x = "Mean within-job white-name minus Black-name contact rate",
    y = "Number of bootstrap samples"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Did changing the resampling unit change the substantive conclusion? What did
it improve about the foundation of the estimate?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

## Does the Pooled Result Describe Every Employer?

Now each group will choose one anonymized employer. Change only the value of
`employer_choice`. Do not choose the employer because you already know its
result.

```{r choose-employer}
# Replace 001 with the three-digit employer number assigned to your group.
employer_choice = "Employer_001"

chosen_employer = large_audit |>
  filter(Employer == employer_choice)

chosen_employer |>
  count(NameRace)
```

Calculate and plot its two contact rates.

```{r chosen-employer-rates}
chosen_employer_rates = chosen_employer |>
  group_by(NameRace) |>
  summarize(
    Applications = n(),
    ContactRate = mean(Contact),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

chosen_employer_rates

chosen_employer_rates |>
  summarize(
    Difference = ContactRate[NameRace == "White"] -
      ContactRate[NameRace == "Black"]
  )

ggplot(
  chosen_employer_rates,
  aes(x = NameRace, y = ContactRate, fill = NameRace)
) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, by = .2),
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Contact Rates for", employer_choice),
    x = "Race signaled by applicant name",
    y = "Employer contact rate"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Now calculate its within-job gaps and bootstrap those jobs. This is the same
analysis as above after one `filter()`.

```{r chosen-employer-bootstrap}
chosen_employer_job_gaps = chosen_employer |>
  group_by(Job) |>
  summarize(
    BlackContact = mean(Contact[NameRace == "Black"]),
    WhiteContact = mean(Contact[NameRace == "White"]),
    Difference = WhiteContact - BlackContact,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(Difference))

set.seed(42)

chosen_employer_bootstrap = NULL

for (i in 1:1000) {
  one_difference = chosen_employer_job_gaps |>
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE) |>
    summarize(Difference = mean(Difference))

  chosen_employer_bootstrap = bind_rows(
    chosen_employer_bootstrap,
    one_difference
  )
}

quantile(
  chosen_employer_bootstrap$Difference,
  probs = c(.025, .975)
)
```

```{r plot-chosen-employer-bootstrap}
ggplot(chosen_employer_bootstrap, aes(x = Difference)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Bootstrap Distribution for", employer_choice),
    subtitle = paste(nrow(chosen_employer_bootstrap), "job-level bootstrap samples"),
    x = "Mean within-job white-name minus Black-name contact rate",
    y = "Number of bootstrap samples"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Report your employer, observed difference, and interval to the class.

- Why did groups obtain different estimates?
- Why are some intervals wider?
- Is the pooled result true of every employer?
- Does a negative estimate establish that an employer favors Black applicants?
- Can we rank the employers using these raw estimates?

YOUR ANSWER HERE:

The paper uses additional methods to distinguish persistent employer
differences from noise. We have not learned those methods. We will not name or
rank employers from these raw differences.

# Return to the Research Designs

Compare the two studies.

- Which study gives us the cleanest estimate of the effect of a criminal
  record?
- Which study gives us the cleanest estimate of employers' responses to a
  racialized name?
- Which study observes race more directly?
- Which study removes differences among individual testers?
- Which study has broader geographic scope?
- What temporal limits remain in both studies?
- What does each outcome measure?
- What uncertainty does the bootstrap address?
- What research-design problems can the bootstrap not repair?

# Works Cited

## Data and Studies

Pager, Devah. 2003. “The Mark of a Criminal Record.” *American Journal of
Sociology* 108(5): 937–975.
[https://doi.org/10.1086/374403](https://doi.org/10.1086/374403).

The course file `criminalrecord.csv` contains 695 applications from Pager's
Milwaukee audit study. Four cases from the published study were redacted.

Pager, Devah, Bruce Western, and Bart Bonikowski. 2009. “Discrimination in a
Low-Wage Labor Market: A Field Experiment.” *American Sociological Review*
74(5): 777–799.
[https://doi.org/10.1177/000312240907400505](https://doi.org/10.1177/000312240907400505).

Kline, Patrick M., Evan K. Rose, and Christopher R. Walters. 2022. “Systemic
Discrimination Among Large U.S. Employers.” *Quarterly Journal of Economics*
137(4): 1963–2036.
[https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjac024](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjac024).

Kline, Patrick M., Evan K. Rose, and Christopher R. Walters. 2022. “Replication
Data for: ‘Systemic Discrimination Among Large U.S. Employers.’” Harvard
Dataverse, version 1.1. CC0 1.0.
[https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/HLO4XC](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/HLO4XC).
The course file
`largeaudit.csv`
retains all applications but only anonymized employer and job identifiers,
state, submission date, the racialized-name treatment, and the contact
outcome. The transformation is
documented and reproduced by
`data/KlineRoseWalters/Prepare_Kline_Rose_Walters_LargeEmployerAudit_TeachingData.R`.
